meal: grilled ribeye steak with a peppercorn cream sauce

baseline_pick.title: Mattucci 2013 Bentley Ironworks Cabernet Sauvignon (Paso Robles)

strategy.target_style: Full-bodied Cabernet Sauvignon or Cabernet-led blend from California or Washington, firm ripe tannins, good acidity, recent vintage, around $45
strategy.search_query: full-bodied Cabernet Sauvignon firm tannins structured fresh acidity black currant cassis cedar black pepper spice savory
strategy.rationale: A ribeye's marbled fat and char call for a full-bodied Cabernet whose firm tannins grip the fat and whose acidity cuts the cream sauce, while the black pepper and cassis notes in the wine echo the peppercorns, and it matches the American steakhouse setting.

Viña Requingua 2012 Potro de Piedra Family Reserve Single Vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon-Cabernet Franc (Curicó Valley)

recommendation:
For this ribeye with peppercorn cream, I'd pick these two:

**JD 2007 Cabernet Sauvignon, Diamond Mountain District (94 pts, $40) [5].** It's the closest match to the target: a California Cabernet near $45 with "tightly wound mountain tannins" that will grip the marbled fat and clean the palate between bites. Its blackberry, black currant and cedar sit well against the char, and the wine is still fresh enough to cut through the cream sauce. It's an older vintage, but the review says it's approachable now and will keep for years.

**Sineann 2012 Cabernet Sauvignon, Columbia Valley, WA (94 pts, $30) [3].** This is the Washington option, riper and more concentrated, and it costs less. The dense black fruit has the body to hold up to a rich steak. The coffee and molasses running through its tannins go with the grill char, and the baking-spice notes pick up the cracked pepper in the sauce.

If you want one bottle, take the JD [5]. Its firmer tannins and cedar structure handle the fat better than the plusher Sineann does.

issues: The 2007 JD will be about 19 years old in 2026. Its tannins have probably softened since release, so a review from release time saying they are 'tightly wound' and will 'grip the marbled fat' may no longer hold.
Cutting through a cream sauce is mostly acidity's job. The note credits the wine's freshness without naming its acidity, and a mature mountain Cabernet may not have much lift left.
The Sineann's molasses, coffee and ripe fruit could feel heavy next to a rich cream sauce. Without acidity to balance it, the pairing can turn cloying.
Black pepper pulls toward Syrah. A Northern Rhône or Washington Syrah would match the peppercorn more directly, and the note doesn't mention that option.
The $40 price is probably the release price. A 2007 bottle will likely cost more now, or be hard to find.

meal: raw oysters on the half shell with mignonette

strategy.target_style: Bone-dry, unoaked, high-acid coastal white with saline minerality: Muscadet Sèvre et Maine sur lie, Picpoul de Pinet, or a Brut Champagne/Crémant
strategy.search_query: Muscadet sur lie or Picpoul de Pinet or brut Crémant, bone-dry unoaked crisp, saline, sea spray, chalky minerality, lemon, green apple, high acidity
strategy.rationale: Oysters and a vinegar mignonette need a lean, unoaked, high-acid white with saline minerality; oak tends to turn metallic against the oyster's iodine, and ripe fruit tastes sweet next to the brine, while Muscadet, Picpoul and dry Crémant usually sell for under $30 and avoid both problems.

candidates.title: Trisaetum 2015 Coast Range Estate Dry Riesling
Markus Huber 2016 Engelsberg Riesling (Traisental)
Domaine Zind-Humbrecht 2015 Goldert Grand Cru Muscat (Alsace)
Neumeister 2016 Steirische Klassik Gelber Muskateller
Salomon-Undhof 2016 Stein a.d. Donau Riesling (Kremstal)
Paul O'Brien 2013 Bone Dry Riesling (Umpqua Valley)

recommendation:
None of the six wines is a Muscadet, Picpoul or Champagne, so I've picked the two closest to that lean, salty style.

**Salomon-Undhof 2016 Stein a.d. Donau Riesling (Kremstal), 91 pts, $25 [5]**
This is the closest match to a Muscadet sur lie. The review calls it "taut, dry, slender" and notes a yeasty, "almost-salty texture" with a bright lemon streak, which suits the brine of the oyster. Its light body won't swamp a raw oyster, and its acidity is high enough to hold up against the red wine vinegar in the mignonette.

**Paul O'Brien 2013 Bone Dry Riesling (Umpqua Valley), 92 pts, $26 [6]**
Pick this one if you like more acid. It's bone dry and "searingly tart," and the review describes stony notes along with lime and grapefruit. That sharp citrus works the way a squeeze of lemon does on an oyster, and with no oak or sweetness, the iodine won't taste metallic and the brine won't make the fruit taste sweet.

I left out the two Muscats [3, 4] because their floral, peachy perfume would compete with the shallot and pepper.

issues: Vintage age is not addressed: by 2026 the 2013 Oregon and 2016 Kremstal Rieslings may have developed petrol or kerosene notes, which can clash with raw oyster brine and undercut the 'lean Muscadet-like' rationale

Riesling is an aromatic grape with more fruit than Muscadet or Picpoul, so calling it the 'closest match to a Muscadet sur lie' overstates the similarity; the pairing works on acid and dryness, not on style
'Searingly tart' wine next to a red wine vinegar mignonette risks stacking acid on acid, so the wine may taste thin or sour; this deserves a caveat instead of being pitched as the bonus pick
The claim that brine 'won't make the fruit taste sweet' has no clear basis; salt usually softens perceived bitterness and acidity, it doesn't add sweetness
The iodine/metallic argument is mostly about tannin and red wine, not oak in a white, so it is a weak justification here

meal: spicy Thai green curry with chicken

strategy.target_style: Off-dry German Riesling Kabinett from a recent vintage (2020 or later), low alcohol (8 to 10% ABV), noticeable residual sugar and bright lime-citrus acidity
strategy.search_query: off-dry Riesling Kabinett Mosel young fresh lime green apple white peach slightly sweet low alcohol
strategy.rationale: Low alcohol and clear sweetness calm the green chili without adding burn, and young Riesling's lime and green apple fruit sit close to the lime, lemongrass and basil in the curry, which the aged Vouvray and the possibly dry Anjou could not promise.

candidates.title: Markus Molitor 2013 Ürziger Würzgarten Kabinett Riesling (Mosel)
Markus Molitor 2011 Haus Klosterberg Riesling (Mosel)

Sineann 2013 Riesling (Oregon)

recommendation:
None of these six wines meets the 2020-or-later target; the youngest are from 2015. These two come closest.

**Markus Molitor 2013 Ürziger Würzgarten Kabinett Riesling (Mosel), 92 pts, $25 [1].** This is my first pick. The review calls it "feather-light," which in Mosel Kabinett usually means low alcohol, so it won't make the green chili burn more. Its sweet peach and tropical fruit soften the heat, and the lemon-lime acidity sits close to the lime and lemongrass in the curry and keeps the coconut milk from feeling heavy. The review says it drinks well through at least 2025, so it may be close to the end of that window now.

**Dr. Pauly Bergweiler 2015 Bernkasteler Badstube Kabinett Riesling (Mosel), 92 pts, $20 [4].** This is the backup. Its mango, melon and tangerine go well with coconut and Thai basil, and its "mouthwatering acidity" cuts through the richness of the sauce. The review also gives 2025 as the end of its drinking window, so it has the same age concern as [1].

The dry Fritz Haag Trocken [3] doesn't have the sweetness to tame the chili. The Sineann [6] is a dessert wine and would overpower a savory curry. The von Nell-Breuning [5] was meant to be drunk by 2020. None of the reviews give alcohol levels, so the 8 to 10% ABV target can't be confirmed for any of them.

recommendation:
My first pick is the **Weatherborne 2012 Pinot Noir, Sta. Rita Hills (92 pts, $35) [6]**. Its wet-earth, mushroom and shiitake flavors match the wild mushrooms almost exactly. It is soft and elegant in the mouth, with no hard tannin, so it won't taste bitter against the parmesan cream. The savory umami in the wine also matches the umami in the cheese.

For a bit more energy, try the **Wrath 2012 Swan/828 Pinot Noir, Monterey (93 pts, $35) [5]**. The review calls it "a study of umami," with shiitake, loam and soy, so it has the same earthy profile as the risotto. It's silky but has "immediate verve," and that freshness cuts through the rich, creamy rice, so each bite tastes as good as the first.

Neither wine is Nebbiolo, and both are from 2012 instead of a recent vintage. Even so, these two are the closest fit to the forest-floor Pinot style you asked for.

issues: The user asked for Nebbiolo and a recent vintage. Neither request is met, and the reply only says so at the end.
Both wines are 2012 California Pinot at $35, which makes them 14 years old in 2026. They may be past peak, with the fruit faded, and nothing in the reply checks their current condition.
Pinot Noir is lighter-bodied than a rich parmesan-cream risotto. A riper, fuller Pinot or a white with some oak, such as Chardonnay or white Burgundy, would match the weight better.
The claim that the wine's umami matches the cheese is loose. Wine has little real umami, and umami can make red wine taste more bitter. The low tannin is what actually keeps this pairing safe.
The two picks are nearly the same style, so they offer little real choice. An Italian option such as Nebbiolo/Langhe, Barbera or Fiano would suit the cuisine better.
